newsitem.title: USA: Chemical treaty faces likely "killer" amendments.
newsitem.headline: Chemical treaty faces likely "killer" amendments.

text.p: A Senate proponent of a global treaty outlawing chemical weapons said Tuesday that most issues raised by critics had been resolved but that four "killer" amendments would probably be voted on by the Senate.
The Senate is expected to debate the Chemical Weapons Convention next week as the Clinton administration pushes for approval before April 29 when it goes into force.

Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware, senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Comittee, told reporters that in lengthy negotiations with Committee Chairman Jesse Helms of North Carolina, a foe of the treaty, tentative agreement had been reached on 23 of 33 conditions.
Any of four of the 10 proposed conditions remaining could kill U.S. participation in the treaty, Biden said.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said he expected the treaty to come before the Senate next week after the Senate deals with a separate bill under which the United States would take a go-it-alone approach to combating the spread of chemical weapons.
That bill, proposed by Arizona Republican Jon Kyl, will go before the Senate on Thursday, Lott told reporters.

Lott said that he was near reaching agreement on timing and terms of debate on the treaty. Under Senate rules, this requires the unanimous consent of senators, including Helms, who has made clear that he is in no hurry for a Senate vote.

Helms held further hearings on the pact Tuesday, with former Republican presidential contender Steve Forbes telling the committee: "This treaty is not worth the paper it is written on, the way it is now."
Biden told reporters that the crucial amendments likely to be voted on by the Senate would:
- Bar the United States from participation in the treaty until so-called "rogue" states, such as Iraq and Libya, were included.
- Raise the standards of verification against cheating to unachievable levels.
- Link U.S. participation to Russian ratification of the pact and compliance with an earlier agreement to destroy its poison gas stocks.
- Require renegotiation of treaty articles requiring exchange of information on chemical weapons defences and on chemical trade.
Approval of the treaty requires a two-thirds majority. Votes on amendments to the resolution of ratification require only a simple majority.
Biden called the Kyl bill a "wild card" in the treaty debate, saying it was unclear how it would affect the vote on the treaty. He said the bill faced a presidential veto if it passed Congress.
Biden called again on Lott to get the treaty free from Helms's grip, saying: "His leadership is literally in the balance, at least in foreign policy."
Lott, asked by reporters, how he was dealing with Helms on the treaty, said, "Gingerly."
